<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:vi-main}
For $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, a solution $z_\star$ satisfies for all $z\in\mathbb R^d$
\[
 \langle F(z_\star),z-z_\star\rangle\ge0\;
 \;\Longleftrightarrow\;F(z_\star)=0.
\]
The algorithm starts from $z_0$ and does not know the root $z_\star$.
For the affine and composite models of
Sections~\ref{sec:affine-integrated} and~\ref{sec:acceleration-main}
we write $(G,x_0,x_\star)$ instead of $(F,z_0,z_\star)$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:monotone-lipschitz}
Let $L>0$. The map $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ has a root
$z_\star$ and satisfies, for all $z,u\in\mathbb R^d$,
\[
 \langle F(z)-F(u),z-u\rangle\ge0,
 \quad \|F(z)-F(u)\|\le L\|z-u\|.
\]
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- assumption-2: body_md -->
\label{ass:strong-monotonicity}
For $\mu>0$, the map $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfies for all $z,u\in\mathbb R^d$
\[
 \langle F(z)-F(u),z-u\rangle\ge\mu\|z-u\|^2.
\]
<!-- end assumption-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:ic-main}
Fix $m,K,N\in\mathbb N$. An algorithm runs on $m$ workers for $N$
communication rounds. In each
round, every worker makes at most $K$ sequential oracle calls; a query
may depend on the information shared at the start of the round, on the
worker's own randomness, and on its earlier responses in that round.
Workers communicate only at round boundaries. Messages, memory, and
local computation are unrestricted. Query and output maps are Borel
measurable and may take arbitrary finite values, and the randomness of
the algorithm is independent of the instance and of the oracle.

 
                                                   On a sample space $\Xi$,    all workers query the same oracle
$g:\mathbb R^d\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^d$.  
                                                   At each call, $\xi$
is drawn from a fixed law independently of all   
earlier draws and of the algorithm's randomness; the query is
measurable with respect to the information $\mathcal F$ available
before the call. Every call counts towards the budget, including both
calls of an extragradient step. Our algorithms may use the model
parameters. We call any randomized algorithm satisfying these rules
\emph{admissible}. Its output is denoted by $\widehat z$; in the affine
and composite settings, where the problem variable is $x$, the output
is denoted by $\widehat x$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- assumption-3: body_md -->
\label{ass:sgc}
For $\rho\ge1$, every pre-call history $\mathcal F$ and every
$\mathcal F$-measurable query $z\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E[g(z,\xi)\mid\mathcal F]&=F(z),\\
 \mathbb E[\|g(z,\xi)\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
 &\le\rho\|F(z)\|^2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end assumption-3 -->
<!-- assumption-4: body_md -->
\label{ass:mixed}
For $\rho\ge1$ and $\sigma\ge0$, every pre-call history $\mathcal F$
and every $\mathcal F$-measurable query $z\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E[g(z,\xi)\mid\mathcal F]&=F(z),\\
 \mathbb E[\|g(z,\xi)-F(z)\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
 &\le(\rho-1)\|F(z)\|^2+\sigma^2.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
<!-- end assumption-4 -->
<!-- assumption-5: body_md -->
\label{ass:interpolation}
Let $F(z_\star)=0$. The oracle $g:\mathbb R^d\times\Xi\to\mathbb R^d$
satisfies
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbb E_\xi g(z,\xi)=F(z)\quad(\forall z\in\mathbb R^d),\\
 \sigma_\star^2:=\mathbb E_\xi\|g(z_\star,\xi)\|^2<\infty.
 \end{gathered}
\]
Interpolation is the case $\sigma_\star=0$, that is,
\begin{equation*}
 g(z_\star,\xi)=0\qquad\text{almost surely}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end assumption-5 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:noise-contracts-main}
Unbiasedness gives
\[
 \mathbb E[\|g(z,\xi)\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
 =\|F(z)\|^2+
   \mathbb E[\|g(z,\xi)-F(z)\|^2\mid\mathcal F].
\]
Hence SGC is the mixed condition with $\sigma=0$, and it implies
interpolation at every root. Interpolation does not imply SGC
 
                                                   even for smooth convex sample losses   . In the mixed model, $\sigma^2$ is
an additive budget: the variance at $z$ is at most
$(\rho-1)\|F(z)\|^2+\sigma^2$, which exceeds $\sigma^2$ away from the
roots when $\rho>1$, while the variance at a root is
$\sigma_\star^2\le\sigma^2$. For $\rho=1$, $\sigma^2$ bounds the variance at
every query and the mixed model is the bounded-variance model.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:gaps-main}
For a nonempty compact set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ containing a root,
the Minty gap is
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{Gap}_C^{\rm M}(z)
 :=\sup_{u\in C}\langle F(u),z-u\rangle.
\end{equation*}
For nonlinear VIs the test set satisfies
$z_\star\in C\subseteq B(z_0,D)$ with $D>0$. For a differentiable
convex--concave $\Phi(x,y)$, $F=(\nabla_x\Phi,-\nabla_y\Phi)$, and
compact sets $X,Y$ whose product contains a saddle point, the
primal--dual gap is
\[
 \operatorname{Gap}^{\rm PD}_{X\times Y}(x,y)
 :=\sup_{v\in Y}\Phi(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}\Phi(u,y).
\]
We always keep the superscripts ${\rm M}$ and ${\rm PD}$. All expected-gap
bounds place the supremum inside the expectation. The test set restricts
neither queries nor outputs.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- assumption-6: body_md -->
\label{ass:affine-main}
 
                                                   Let $L,R_0>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, and
$J\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $J+J^\top\succeq0$. The operator
$G:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ has an unknown root $x_\star$ and satisfies   
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 G(x)=J(x-x_\star),\quad \|x_0-x_\star\|\le R_0, \quad
 \|J\|_{\rm op}\le L.
\end{gathered}
\]
The initial point $x_0$ and the radius $R_0$ are known; $J$ and the root
$x_\star$ are not. The sampled maps need not be affine.
<!-- end assumption-6 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:affine-risks-main}
Let $\mathcal E_d^{\rm aff,rel}$ and $\mathcal E_d^{\rm aff,mix}$ be the
minimax values, over the algorithms of Definition~\ref{def:ic-main}, of
the expected root-centered Minty gap $\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)$
over Assumption~\ref{ass:affine-main} combined with
Assumption~\ref{ass:sgc} and with Assumption~\ref{ass:mixed},
respectively, for $F=G$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:aff:self-contained-gap}
 \operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(x)=\sup_{\|u-x_\star\|\le R_0}
                       \langle G(u),x-u\rangle .
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:affine-integrated}\label{thm:pure-affine-main}\label{pv:minimax}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:affine-main} and~\ref{ass:sgc}, for every
$m,K,N\in\mathbb N$, $L,R_0>0$, and $\rho\ge1$, there is a finite
dimension $d_{\rm hard}=O\bigl(m(KN)^2\bigr)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal E_{d_{\rm hard}}^{\rm aff,rel}
 =\Theta\!\left(\frac{LR_0^2}{1+ND_{\mathrm{info}}}\right).
\end{equation*}
The upper bound holds in every finite dimension. The lower bound uses
one fixed distribution of affine operators with unique roots.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:affine-additive-main}\label{thm:affine-mixed-main}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:affine-main} and~\ref{ass:mixed}, for every
$m,K,N\in\mathbb N$, $L,R_0>0$, $\rho\ge1$, and $\sigma\ge0$, there is a
finite dimension $d_{\rm mix}=O\bigl(m(KN)^2\bigr)$ such that
\begin{equation*}
 \mathcal E_{d_{\rm mix}}^{\rm aff,mix}
 =\widetilde\Theta\!\Biggl(R_0^2\min\Biggl\{L,\ 
 \frac{L}{N}\min\!\left\{\frac\rho K,1+\frac\rho{mK}\right\}
 +\frac{\sigma}{R_0\sqrt{mKN}}\Biggr\}\Biggr).
\end{equation*}
where the upper bound holds up to a universal constant, in every finite
dimension, and the lower bound up to a universal multiple of $\log(2m)$. The hard
instances may have root noise exactly $\sigma^2$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{vi:main-monotone}
Let Assumptions~\ref{ass:monotone-lipschitz} and~\ref{ass:sgc} hold,
let $D>0$, and let $C$ be a nonempty compact set with
$z_\star\in C\subseteq B(z_0,D)$.
 
                                                   There exists an admissible algorithm attaining   
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^{\rm M}(\widehat z)
 =O\!\left(\frac{LD^2}{1+ND_{\mathrm{sched}}}\right)
\end{equation*}
for the Minty gap. If
$F=(\nabla_x\Phi,-\nabla_y\Phi)$ for a differentiable convex--concave
$\Phi$ and $C=X\times Y$ is a product set, its expected primal--dual
gap $\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_{X\times Y}^{\rm PD}(\widehat z)$ satisfies the same bound.

Conversely,  
                                                   in a sufficiently large finite dimension,    every
admissible algorithm has an instance in this class,
with a root in $B(z_0,D)$, such that
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}^{\rm M}_{B(z_0,D)}(\widehat z)
 =\Omega\!\left(\frac{LD^2}{1+ND_{\mathrm{info}}}\right).
\end{equation*}
For saddle problems, one $C^2$ convex--concave instance satisfies the
same lower bound for both gaps on the product of the two balls of
radius $D/\sqrt2$ centered at the blocks of $z_0$, which contains its
root. The lower bounds hold
even if every response reveals whether it is informative and, for
saddle problems, the sample values. The sample operators share the root
and are $\rho L$-Lipschitz.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{vi:main-mixed}
Let Assumption~\ref{ass:mixed} hold with $\rho\ge1$ and $\sigma\ge0$,
together with the remaining conditions of Theorem~\ref{vi:main-monotone}.
Set
\begin{equation*}
 r_{\rm mix}:=\min\Biggl\{L,\ 
 \frac{\rho L}{KN}+\frac{\sigma}{D\sqrt{KN}},\ 
 \frac{L}{N}\left(1+\frac{\rho}{mK}\right)
                  +\frac{\sigma}{D\sqrt{mKN}}\Biggr\}.
\end{equation*}
 
                                                   There exists an admissible algorithm attaining   
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^{\rm M}(\widehat z)=O(D^2r_{\rm mix}).
\end{equation*}
For a saddle problem with $C=X\times Y$, it also satisfies
$\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_{X\times Y}^{\rm PD}(\widehat z)=O(D^2r_{\rm mix})$.
Conversely,  
                                                   in a sufficiently large finite dimension,    every
admissible algorithm has an instance in this class,
with a root in $B(z_0,D)$, such that
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}^{\rm M}_{B(z_0,D)}(\widehat z)
 =\Omega\!\left(\frac{D^2r_{\rm mix}}{\log(2m)}\right).
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{vi:main-mixed-accuracy}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:monotone-lipschitz},
\ref{ass:strong-monotonicity}, and~\ref{ass:mixed}, let $\kappa\ge2$ and
$\|z_0-z_\star\|\le R_0$. For a universal constant $c>0$ let
$K_{\rm cq}=\min\{1,mK/\rho\}$ and
$\bar m_N=m/(1+m\,e^{-cNK_{\rm cq}/\kappa})$. There exists an admissible
algorithm attaining
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2\lesssim\min\Bigl\{R_0^2,\
 R_0^2e^{-cND_{\mathrm{sched}}/\kappa}
 +\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2\bar m_NKN}\Bigr\}.
\end{equation*}
Conversely, for universal constants $C,c'>0$ let $m_N=1$ if
$N\log(2m)\le c'\kappa$ and $m_N=m$ otherwise. In a sufficiently large
finite dimension, every admissible algorithm has an instance in this
class with
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2\gtrsim\max\Bigl\{
 R_0^2e^{-CND_{\mathrm{info}}/\kappa},\
 \min\Bigl\{R_0^2,\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2m_NKN}\Bigr\}\Bigr\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- assumption-7: body_md -->
\label{ass:generalized-smoothness}
Let $L_0,R_0>0$ and $L_1\ge0$. The operator
$F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is continuously differentiable. Writing
$\mathrm DF(z)$ for its Jacobian at $z$, we require, for every
$z,u\in\mathbb R^d$,
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{aligned}
 \langle F(z)-F(u),z-u\rangle&\ge0,\\
 \|\mathrm DF(z)\|_{\rm op}&\le L_0+L_1\|F(z)\|.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
There is a root $z_\star$ with
$F(z_\star)=0$ and $\|z_0-z_\star\|\le R_0$.
<!-- end assumption-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{gs:main-distance-complexity}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:generalized-smoothness},
\ref{ass:strong-monotonicity}, and~\ref{ass:sgc}, let $\kappa_0=L_0/\mu\ge1$,
$\vartheta=\min\{\rho/K,1+\rho/(mK)\}$, and
$\ell_0=\log(64\max\{(1+L_1R_0)^2,\kappa_0\})$. For every $N\ge1$ and a
universal constant $c>0$, an admissible adaptive restarted extragradient
method satisfies, in every finite dimension,
$\mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2\le8R_0^2e^{-cx_N}$ with
\begin{equation*}
 x_N=\min\Bigl\{\frac{N}{\ell_0\bigl(1+\vartheta(L_1R_0)^2\bigr)},\
 \sqrt{\frac{N}{\ell_0\vartheta\kappa_0}}\Bigr\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- assumption-8: body_md -->
\label{ass:interp-main}
Let $d\in\mathbb N$, $R_0>0$, $0\le L_f\le L_{\max}<\infty$, and
$0\le L_H<\infty$. On $\mathbb R^d$, let
\[
 G=\nabla f+H,
\]
where $f$ is convex with an $L_f$-Lipschitz gradient, and $H$ is
deterministic, monotone, and $L_H$-Lipschitz. A designated root satisfies
\[
 G(x_\star)=0,\qquad \|x_0-x_\star\|\le R_0.
\]
Almost every sample function $f_\xi$ is convex on $\mathbb R^d$ and has
an $L_{\max}$-Lipschitz gradient. At every query $x$ measurable with
respect to the pre-call history $\mathcal F$,  
                                                   the sample drawn
for that call is independent of $\mathcal F$    and
\[
 \mathbb E[\nabla f_\xi(x)\mid\mathcal F]=\nabla f(x).
\]
All workers use the same sample distribution and the same exact map $H$;
samples are independent across calls and workers, and all maps and
outputs are measurable. The root noise is finite:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composite-root-variance-main}
 \sigma_\star^2
 :=\mathbb E\|\nabla f_\xi(x_\star)+H(x_\star)\|^2
 =\mathbb E\|\nabla f_\xi(x_\star)-\nabla f(x_\star)\|^2<\infty.
\end{equation}
One stochastic gradient or one evaluation of $H$ costs one call.
Algorithms know the displayed parameters; an upper bound on
$\sigma_\star$ may replace its exact value.
<!-- end assumption-8 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define
\begin{equation*}
 \operatorname{Gap}_{R_0}^{\mathrm{comp}}(x)
 =\sup_{\|u-x_\star\|\le R_0}
   \{f(x)-f(u)+\langle H(u),x-u\rangle\}.
\end{equation*}
The error is $\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_{R_0}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat x)$, with the
expectation outside the supremum.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:composite-local-main}
Under Assumption~\ref{ass:interp-main}, for every $m,K\ge1$ and $N\ge2$,
 
                                                   there exists an admissible algorithm attaining   
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_{R_0}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat x)=
 \widetilde O\!\Bigl(R_0^2\min\bigl\{L_f+L_H,
 r_{\mathrm{seq}}(\sigma_\star),r_{\mathrm{mb}}(\sigma_\star)\bigr\}\Bigr).
\end{equation*}
 
                                                   The sequential single-worker guarantee has no logarithmic
factors and holds for $N=1$; the parallel-minibatch guarantee hides
powers of $\log(2mKN)$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Fix $L_f,L_H,L_{\max},R_0$ and $m,K,N\in\mathbb N$.
For $\nu\ge0$, let $\mathfrak I_d(\nu)$ be the class of instances of
Assumption~\ref{ass:interp-main} in $\mathbb R^d$ with
\[
 \mathbb E\|\nabla f_\xi(x_\star)+H(x_\star)\|^2\le \nu^2.
\]
 
                                                   Let $\mathsf A$ range over admissible randomized algorithms,
let $\mathcal I$ denote an instance in $\mathfrak I_d(\nu)$, and let
$\mathbb E_{\mathsf A,\mathcal I}$ average over all randomness;
$\mathsf A$ may use $d$ and the model parameters.   
Define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathfrak R_{\rm comp}(\nu)
 :=\sup_{d\in\mathbb N}\inf_{\mathsf A}
       \sup_{\mathcal I\in\mathfrak I_d(\nu)}
       \mathbb E_{\mathsf A,\mathcal I}\operatorname{Gap}_{R_0}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat x),
\end{gathered}
\]
 
                                                   Thus $\mathfrak R_{\rm comp}(0)$ is the interpolation risk.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:composite-lower-main}
\label{interp:explicit-main}
\label{prop:composite-root-budget-main}
Let $0\le L_f\le L_{\max}$, $L_H\ge0$, $R_0>0$, $m,K,N\in\mathbb N$, and
$\nu\ge0$. In a common dimension of at most $2048m(KN)^2$, and in every
larger dimension,
\begin{equation*}
 \begin{multlined}
 \frac{\mathfrak R_{\rm comp}(\nu)}{R_0^2}
 =\Omega\!\Biggl(
 \frac{L_f}{(KN)^2}+\frac{L_H}{KN}
 \!+\!\min\!\left\{L_f,\frac{L_{\max}}{mKN}\right\}\\[-2pt]
 \quad ~ ~ +\min\!\left\{\frac{L_f}{(1+N\log m)^2},
              \frac{L_{\max}}{KN(1+N\log m)}\right\}\\[-2pt]
 \quad+\min\!\left\{L_f+L_H,
              \frac{\nu}{R_0\sqrt{mKN}}\right\}\Biggr).
 \end{multlined}
\end{equation*}
The first four terms are attained by interpolating instances.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:composite-matching-main}\label{comp-proj:matching}
Let $m,K\ge1$, $N\ge2$, $R_0>0$, $\nu\ge0$, $L_H\ge0$, and
$0<KL_f\le L_{\max}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
 \mathfrak R_{\rm comp}(\nu)=
 \widetilde\Theta\!\left(
 R_0^2\min\{L_f+L_H,r_{\mathrm{mb}}(\nu)\}\right),
\end{equation*}
where the tilde hides powers of $\log(2mKN)$. The lower bound holds in
every dimension of at least
$\max\{2048m(KN)^2,\lceil8192L_{\max}/L_f\rceil\}$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:clock:elementary}
For all the above parameters,
\begin{align*}
 \max\{Kp,(1-e^{-1})\min\{1,mKp\}\}
 &\le\beta_p\\
 &\le\min\{K,mKp,(e-1)Kp+\log m\}.\nonumber
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We begin by establishing a lower bound for $\beta_p$. First, observe that
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p = \mathbb E\max_{1\le i\le m} Z_i \ge \mathbb E Z_1 = Kp.
\end{equation*}
On the other hand, let $Z_{\max}=\max_{1\le i\le m}Z_i$. Since
$Z_{\max}\ge1$ on the event $\{Z_{\max}\ge1\}$, we have
$Z_{\max}\ge\mathbf 1_{\{Z_{\max}\ge1\}}$, and therefore
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p = \mathbb E Z_{\max} \ge \mathbb P(Z_{\max} \ge 1).
\end{equation*}
Now,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P(Z_{\max} \ge 1)
&= 1 - \mathbb P(Z_{\max} = 0) = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^m \mathbb P(Z_i = 0) = 1 - (1-p)^{Km} \ge 1 - e^{-mKp},
\end{align*}
where the last inequality follows from $1 - p \le e^{-p}$.

Using the elementary bound $1 - e^{-x} \ge (1 - e^{-1}) \min\{1, x\}$, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p \ge \max\left\{Kp,\ (1 - e^{-1}) \min\{1, mKp\} \right\}.
\end{equation*}

We now turn to the upper bound. It is immediate that
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p \le K
\quad\text{and}\quad
\beta_p \le mKp.
\end{equation*}
Next, note that for any $\eta_{\rm mgf}>0$
\begin{equation*}
e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}Z_{\max}}
=\max_{1\le i\le m}e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}Z_i}
\le\sum_{i=1}^m e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}Z_i}.
\end{equation*}
By Jensen's inequality,
\begin{equation*}
e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}\mathbb E Z_{\max}}
\le \mathbb E e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}Z_{\max}}
\le\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbb E e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}Z_i}
=m\bigl(1+p(e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}}-1)\bigr)^K .
\end{equation*}
Taking logarithms yields
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p
\le \frac{\log m+K\log(1+p(e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}}-1))}{\eta_{\rm mgf}}
\le \frac{\log m+Kp(e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}}-1)}{\eta_{\rm mgf}}.
\end{equation*}
For $\eta_{\rm mgf}=1$ this completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:clock:asymptotic}

Uniformly in all $m,K\ge1$ and $0<p\le1$,
\begin{equation*}
 \frac{D_{\mathrm{bin}}(m,K,p)}{64}\le\beta_p
 \le4D_{\mathrm{bin}}(m,K,p).
\end{equation*}
Consequently, for every $N\ge1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:clock:reciprocal}
 \frac{1+ND_{\mathrm{bin}}(m,K,p)}{64}\le1+N\beta_p
 \le4\bigl(1+ND_{\mathrm{bin}}(m,K,p)\bigr).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Write $a_{\rm clk}=\log(2m)/\log\bigl(2+\log(2m)/(Kp)\bigr)$ and
$T_{\rm clk}=\min\{K,mKp,Kp+a_{\rm clk}\}$.
Using Lemma~\ref{lem:clock:elementary},
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p\le
\frac{\log m+Kp(e^{\eta_{\rm mgf}}-1)}{\eta_{\rm mgf}}.
\end{equation*}
If $\log(2m)/(Kp)\ge1$, take
$\eta_{\rm mgf}=\log\bigl(1+\log(2m)/(Kp)\bigr)$. Since
$\log(2+x)\le2\log(1+x)$ for $x\ge1$, this gives
$\beta_p\le4a_{\rm clk}$. If $\log(2m)/(Kp)<1$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:clock:elementary}
gives $\beta_p\le(e-1)Kp+\log(2m)<3Kp$. In both cases
$\beta_p\le4(Kp+a_{\rm clk})$. Combining with $\beta_p\le K,mKp$
proves the upper bound.

For the lower bound, first suppose $p\ge1/2$. Then
$\beta_p\ge Kp\ge K/2\ge T_{\rm clk}/2$. Suppose henceforth $p<1/2$.
If $Kp\ge\log(2m)/8$, then
$Kp+a_{\rm clk}\le(1+8/\log2)Kp<13Kp$, so
$\beta_p\ge T_{\rm clk}/13$.
It remains to consider $Kp<\log(2m)/8$.
For $x>8$, $\log(2+x)<x/2$, and hence $a_{\rm clk}>2Kp$ and
$T_{\rm clk}\le Kp+a_{\rm clk}<3a_{\rm clk}/2$.
If $T_{\rm clk}\le16$, the elementary lower bound yields
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p\ge(1-e^{-1})\min\{1,mKp\}
\ge\frac{1-e^{-1}}{16}T_{\rm clk}\ge T_{\rm clk}/64.
\end{equation*}
If $T_{\rm clk}>16$, put $t=\lfloor T_{\rm clk}/16\rfloor$.
Then $T_{\rm clk}/32\le t\le K/16$ and $t\le3a_{\rm clk}/32$.
The elementary binomial estimate $\binom Kt\ge(K/t)^t$ and
$\log(1-p)\ge-2p$ imply
\begin{equation*}
p_{\rm tail}:=\mathbb P(Z_1\ge t)\ge\mathbb P(Z_1=t)
\ge(Kp/t)^t e^{-2Kp}.
\end{equation*}
Since $t/(Kp)\le(3/32)\bigl(\log(2m)/(Kp)\bigr)/\log\bigl(2+\log(2m)/(Kp)\bigr)\le2+\log(2m)/(Kp)$,
\begin{equation*}
t\log\bigl(t/(Kp)\bigr)+2Kp
\le t\max\{0,\log(t/(Kp))\}+2Kp
\le\frac{3\log(2m)}{32}+\frac{\log(2m)}{4}=\frac{11\log(2m)}{32}.
\end{equation*}
Here $m\ge2$: otherwise $T_{\rm clk}\le Kp<\log(2m)/8<1$.
Thus $\log m\ge\log(2m)/2$ and $mp_{\rm tail}\ge1$.
Independence now gives
\begin{equation*}
\beta_p\ge t[1-(1-p_{\rm tail})^m]
\ge(1-e^{-1})t
\ge\frac{1-e^{-1}}{32}T_{\rm clk}\ge T_{\rm clk}/64.
\end{equation*}
Inequality~\eqref{eq:clock:reciprocal} follows by multiplying the two
bounds by $N$ and adding one.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:clock:constructive}
For $p=1/\rho$, $\rho\ge1$, recall that
\[
 D_{\mathrm{sched}}=\max\{K/\rho,\min\{mK/\rho,1\}\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \beta_{1/\rho}\le4\left(1+\frac{\log(2m)}{\log(2+\log(2m))}\right)D_{\mathrm{sched}}.
\end{equation*}
The dependence on $m$ is sharp for this comparison: as $m\to\infty$,
choosing $K=\rho=\lceil\log(2m)\rceil$ gives
\[
 \frac{\beta_{1/\rho}}{D_{\mathrm{sched}}}
 =\Theta\!\left(1+\frac{\log(2m)}{\log(2+\log(2m))}\right).
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write $K_{\rm eff}=K/\rho$. If $mK_{\rm eff}\le1$, then
$D_{\mathrm{sched}}=mK_{\rm eff}$ and
Lemma~\ref{lem:clock:elementary} gives $\beta_{1/\rho}\le D_{\mathrm{sched}}$.
Suppose $mK_{\rm eff}>1$. If $K_{\rm eff}\le1$, then
$D_{\mathrm{sched}}=1$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:clock:asymptotic} gives
\[
 \beta_{1/\rho}\le4\left(K_{\rm eff}
 +\frac{\log(2m)}{\log(2+\log(2m)/K_{\rm eff})}\right)
 \le4\left(1+\frac{\log(2m)}{\log(2+\log(2m))}\right).
\]
If $K_{\rm eff}\ge1$, then $D_{\mathrm{sched}}=K_{\rm eff}$ and
\[
 \frac{\beta_{1/\rho}}{D_{\mathrm{sched}}}
 \le4\left(1+\frac{\log(2m)/K_{\rm eff}}
 {\log(2+\log(2m)/K_{\rm eff})}\right)
 \le4\left(1+\frac{\log(2m)}{\log(2+\log(2m))}\right).
\]
The last inequality follows because $x/\log(2+x)$ is increasing for
$x\ge0$: its derivative has the sign of
$\log(2+x)-x/(2+x)>0$.
For sharpness, take $K=\rho=\lceil\log(2m)\rceil$, so
$K_{\rm eff}=D_{\mathrm{sched}}=1$.
For all sufficiently large $m$, both caps $K$ and $m$ exceed
$1+\log(2m)/\log(2+\log(2m))$. The lower estimate in
Theorem~\ref{thm:clock:asymptotic} completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:gaussian-testing}
Let $Q_{\rm tot}\in\mathbb N$, $\mu_{\rm obs}\ge0$, and $\sigma>0$.
Under two hypotheses $s_{\rm hyp}\in\{-1,1\}$, observe independent
random variables
$Y_j\sim\mathcal N(s_{\rm hyp}\mu_{\rm obs},\sigma^2)$,
$j=1,\ldots,Q_{\rm tot}$. Let $\mathbb P_+$ and $\mathbb P_-$ denote
probability under $s_{\rm hyp}=1$ and $s_{\rm hyp}=-1$, respectively.
Let $\mathcal T$ be any measurable function
of these observations and an independent random seed whose law does not
depend on $s_{\rm hyp}$. Every test
$\widehat s_{\rm hyp}=\widehat s_{\rm hyp}(\mathcal T)\in\{-1,1\}$
satisfies
\[
 \frac{\mathbb P_{+}\{\widehat s_{\rm hyp}=-1\}
       +\mathbb P_{-}\{\widehat s_{\rm hyp}=1\}}2
 \ge\frac12\left(1-
       \frac{\mu_{\rm obs}\sqrt{Q_{\rm tot}}}{\sigma}\right).
\]
In particular, the right side is at least $3/8$ if
$Q_{\rm tot}\mu_{\rm obs}^2/\sigma^2\le1/16$, and at least $7/16$ if
$Q_{\rm tot}\mu_{\rm obs}^2/\sigma^2\le1/64$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Write $P_{s_{\rm hyp}}$ for the product law of the $Q_{\rm tot}$
observations. Direct
integration of the Gaussian log-likelihood ratio gives
\[
 D_{\rm KL}(P_+\Vert P_-)
 =Q_{\rm tot}\frac{(2\mu_{\rm obs})^2}{2\sigma^2}
 =\frac{2Q_{\rm tot}\mu_{\rm obs}^2}{\sigma^2}.
\]
Independent randomization does not change this divergence. Data
processing and Pinsker's inequality therefore imply
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(\mathcal L_+(\mathcal T),
                         \mathcal L_-(\mathcal T))
 \le\operatorname{TV}(P_+,P_-)
 \le\sqrt{\tfrac12D_{\rm KL}(P_+\Vert P_-)}
 =\frac{\mu_{\rm obs}\sqrt{Q_{\rm tot}}}{\sigma}.
\]
For $A=\{\widehat s_{\rm hyp}=1\}$, the average error is
$[1-P_+(A)+P_-(A)]/2\ge[1-\operatorname{TV}]/2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:gaussian-adaptive}
Suppose every response has the form
$g(x)=r_{\rm known}(x)+s_{\rm hyp}\mu_{\rm obs}+\sigma\zeta$, where
$r_{\rm known}$ is known and $\zeta\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ is independent,
possibly as one coordinate of a vector whose other coordinates are known
deterministic functions of the query. (It is not enough that they do not
depend on $s_{\rm hyp}$: an extra coordinate equal to $\zeta$ would reveal
$s_{\rm hyp}$ from one call.) Then
$Y=g(x)-r_{\rm known}(x)
\sim\mathcal N(s_{\rm hyp}\mu_{\rm obs},\sigma^2)$ independently of the
query, and the transcript of an algorithm with at most $Q_{\rm tot}$ calls
is a measurable function of $Y_1,\ldots,Y_{Q_{\rm tot}}$ and of the
algorithm's seed. Hence
Lemma~\ref{lem:gaussian-testing} applies to every adaptive algorithm.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{nn:identity-lemma}
For every $u\in\mathbb R^d$,
\begin{equation}\label{nn:identity}
 2\gamma\langle F(y),y-u\rangle
 =\|x-u\|^2-\|x^+-u\|^2+\gamma^2\mathcal R_{\rm eg}
 -2\gamma\bigl\langle\delta,\,x-\gamma F(y)-u\bigr\rangle,
\end{equation}
where
$\mathcal R_{\rm eg}=-\|F_x+e\|^2+\|F(y)-F_x-e\|^2+\|\delta\|^2$.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{nn:pathwise-residual}
 \gamma^2\mathcal R_{\rm eg}\le-(1-2q_{\rm eg})\gamma^2\|F_x+e\|^2
       +2\gamma^2\|e\|^2+\gamma^2\|\delta\|^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Expanding the square,
\[
 \|x-u\|^2-\|x^+-u\|^2
 =2\gamma\langle F(y)+\delta,x-u\rangle-\gamma^2\|F(y)+\delta\|^2.
\]
Since $x-y=\gamma(F_x+e)$,
\[
 2\gamma\langle F(y),y-u\rangle
 =2\gamma\langle F(y),x-u\rangle-2\gamma^2\langle F(y),F_x+e\rangle .
\]
Subtracting the two displays and expanding
$\|F(y)+\delta\|^2=\|F(y)\|^2+2\langle F(y),\delta\rangle+\|\delta\|^2$,
\[
 2\gamma\langle F(y),y-u\rangle
 -\bigl(\|x-u\|^2-\|x^+-u\|^2\bigr)
 =\gamma^2\bigl(\|F(y)\|^2-2\langle F(y),F_x+e\rangle+\|\delta\|^2\bigr)
 -2\gamma\langle\delta,x-\gamma F(y)-u\rangle .
\]
The bracket equals
$\|F(y)-F_x-e\|^2-\|F_x+e\|^2+\|\delta\|^2=\mathcal R_{\rm eg}$, which
proves~\eqref{nn:identity}. For~\eqref{nn:pathwise-residual}, Lipschitz
continuity gives $\|F(y)-F_x\|\le L\|y-x\|=\gamma L\|F_x+e\|$, hence
\[
 \|F(y)-F_x-e\|^2\le2\|F(y)-F_x\|^2+2\|e\|^2
 \le2q_{\rm eg}\|F_x+e\|^2+2\|e\|^2 .
\]
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{nn:one-step}
\label{vi:seg-one-step}
Assume~\eqref{eq:eg-moments}, $\alpha_{\rm rel}\le1/4$ and
$0<\gamma\le1/(4L)$. Then
for every $u$ that is $\mathcal F$-measurable,
\begin{align}
 \mathbb E[\|x^+-u\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
 &\le\|x-u\|^2-2\gamma\,\mathbb E[\langle F(y),y-u\rangle\mid\mathcal F]
       -\frac7{128}\gamma^2\|F(x)\|^2+\frac{69}{32}\gamma^2\sigma_b^2,
       \label{nn:energy}\\
 \mathbb E[\|\delta\|^2\mid\mathcal F]
 &\le\frac{69}{32}\alpha_{\rm rel}\|F(x)\|^2
      +\frac{33}{32}\sigma_b^2.
       \label{nn:corrector}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
All expectations are conditional on $\mathcal F$. Let
$v_e=\mathbb E\|e\|^2\le \alpha_{\rm rel}\|F_x\|^2+\sigma_b^2$.
Since $e$ is centered and
$\|F(y)-F_x\|\le\gamma L\|F_x+e\|$,
\[
 \mathbb E\|F_x+e\|^2=\|F_x\|^2+v_e,\qquad
 \mathbb E\|F(y)-F_x\|^2\le q_{\rm eg}(\|F_x\|^2+v_e),\qquad
 \mathbb E\|F(y)\|^2\le2\|F_x\|^2+2q_{\rm eg}(\|F_x\|^2+v_e).
\]

\emph{Corrector.} By~\eqref{eq:eg-moments} and the last bound,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E\|\delta\|^2&\le \alpha_{\rm rel}\mathbb E\|F(y)\|^2+\sigma_b^2\\
 &\le2\alpha_{\rm rel}(1+q_{\rm eg})\|F_x\|^2
    +2\alpha_{\rm rel}q_{\rm eg}v_e+\sigma_b^2\\
 &\le2\alpha_{\rm rel}\bigl(1+q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})\bigr)
       \|F_x\|^2+(1+2\alpha_{\rm rel}q_{\rm eg})\sigma_b^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For $\alpha_{\rm rel}\le1/4$ and $q_{\rm eg}\le1/16$ we have
$2(1+q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel}))\le69/32$ and
$1+2\alpha_{\rm rel}q_{\rm eg}\le33/32$, which is~\eqref{nn:corrector}.

\emph{Energy.} Using $\|r-e\|^2\le2\|r\|^2+2\|e\|^2$ with
$r=F(y)-F_x$ and the corrector bound,
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb E\mathcal R_{\rm eg}
 &\le-\bigl(\|F_x\|^2+v_e\bigr)
       +2q_{\rm eg}(\|F_x\|^2+v_e)+2v_e
       +\alpha_{\rm rel}\bigl(2\|F_x\|^2
          +2q_{\rm eg}(\|F_x\|^2+v_e)\bigr)+\sigma_b^2\\
 &=\bigl(-1+2\alpha_{\rm rel}+2q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})\bigr)
       \|F_x\|^2
   +\bigl(1+2q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})\bigr)v_e+\sigma_b^2\\
 &\le\bigl(-1+3\alpha_{\rm rel}
       +2q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})^2\bigr)\|F_x\|^2
       +2\bigl(1+q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})\bigr)\sigma_b^2,
\end{align*}
where the last step uses
$v_e\le \alpha_{\rm rel}\|F_x\|^2+\sigma_b^2$.
For $\alpha_{\rm rel}\le1/4$ and $q_{\rm eg}\le1/16$,
\[
 1-3\alpha_{\rm rel}-2q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})^2
 \ge1-\frac34-\frac{2}{16}\cdot\frac{25}{16}=\frac7{128},
 \qquad 2\bigl(1+q_{\rm eg}(1+\alpha_{\rm rel})\bigr)\le\frac{69}{32}.
\]
The vector $x-\gamma F(y)-u$ is $\mathcal F^+$-measurable and $\delta$ is
centered given $\mathcal F^+$, so the last term of~\eqref{nn:identity}
has zero conditional mean. Taking the conditional expectation
of~\eqref{nn:identity} proves~\eqref{nn:energy}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:aff:batch-model}
Let $A\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}\times d_{\rm sym}}$ be unknown,
and let $b_{\rm rhs}\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}$ be given to the algorithm.
A query at $v$ returns the exact vector $Av$.
Fix integers $w_{\rm batch}\ge1$, $T_{\rm depth}\ge0$, and $c_{\rm out}\ge0$.
In each batch $r=1,\ldots,T_{\rm depth}$, the algorithm chooses
$w_{\rm batch}$ vectors $v_{r,1},\ldots,v_{r,w_{\rm batch}}$ and then receives
$Av_{r,1},\ldots,Av_{r,w_{\rm batch}}$. All queries in a batch are chosen before
any answer from that batch is received. They may depend on $b_{\rm rhs}$ and
all earlier queries and answers. After the last batch, the algorithm
returns $c_{\rm out}$ vectors $z_1,\ldots,z_{c_{\rm out}}$.
Thus $w_{\rm batch}$ is the batch width and $T_{\rm depth}$ is its sequential depth.

All query and output rules are Borel measurable functions of the
available information and internal randomness independent of the
instance. Their norms are unrestricted but finite. Batches containing
fewer than $w_{\rm batch}$ queries are padded with zeros.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:aff:batched}
Consider any algorithm in Definition~\ref{def:aff:batch-model} applied to
\eqref{eq:aff:marked-matrix}. Its original experiment can be realized
jointly with $w_{\rm batch}T_{\rm depth}+c_{\rm out}$ independent standard Gaussian vectors
in $\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}$,
\[
 v^{\rm G}_{r,i},\quad 1\le r\le T_{\rm depth},\ 1\le i\le w_{\rm batch},
 \qquad
 v^{\rm G}_{{\rm out},i},\quad 1\le i\le c_{\rm out},
\]
so that, almost surely, each output satisfies
\begin{align}
 U^\top z_\ell\in\mathcal K_{T_{\rm depth}}:={}&
 \operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^j b_{\rm spec}:0\le j\le T_{\rm depth}\}
+\sum_{r=1}^{T_{\rm depth}}\sum_{i=1}^{w_{\rm batch}}
   \operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^j v^{\rm G}_{r,i}:0\le j\le T_{\rm depth}-r+1\}
 \nonumber\\
 &+\operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{{\rm out},i}:1\le i\le c_{\rm out}\}.
 \label{eq:aff:krylov}
\end{align}
The joint law of the instance, queries, answers, and outputs is unchanged.
The matrix $U$ has Haar law and is independent of the algorithm's
internal randomness. The Gaussian collection has its independent
product law and is also independent of the algorithm's internal
randomness. The collection and $U$ may depend on one another.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix the algorithm's internal random choices. We construct $U$ by
specifying its action only as needed. If that action is specified on
$E$, the remaining map from $E^\perp$ to $(UE)^\perp$ is conditionally
uniform. We use the following standard Haar property from the cited
conditioning argument: the inverse images of a fixed orthonormal
frame in $(UE)^\perp$ form a uniform orthonormal frame in $E^\perp$;
after these images are specified, the remaining map is still uniform.
Such an inverse frame is obtained by projecting independent standard
Gaussian vectors onto $E^\perp$ and applying Gram--Schmidt
(successive orthogonal projection and normalization).
The same property applies to images of a reference-coordinate frame.

\emph{Initial information.}
Set $E_0=\operatorname{span}\{b_{\rm spec}\}$.
For $b_{\rm spec}\ne0$, draw $b_{\rm rhs}$ uniformly on the sphere of radius
$\|b_{\rm spec}\|$ and specify $Ub_{\rm spec}=b_{\rm rhs}$.
For $b_{\rm spec}=0$, set $b_{\rm rhs}=0$ and $E_0=\{0\}$.
In either case this is the original law of the supplied vector,
and the remaining rotation is conditionally uniform.

\emph{One batch.}
Suppose $U$ is specified on $E=E_{r-1}$, and put $S=UE$.
The queries $v_{r,1},\ldots,v_{r,w_{\rm batch}}$ are already determined.
Choose an orthonormal basis $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ of
\[
 \operatorname{span}\{(I-\Pi_S)v_{r,i}:1\le i\le w_{\rm batch}\},
 \qquad k\le\min\{w_{\rm batch},d_{\rm sym}-\dim E\}.
\]
Draw $v^{\rm G}_{r,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{r,w_{\rm batch}}$
independently of everything generated
so far. Project the first $k$ draws onto $E^\perp$ and orthonormalize
them to obtain $\widetilde u_1,\ldots,\widetilde u_k$.
Specify $U\widetilde u_j=u_j$. Since
\[
 \widetilde u_j\in E+\operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{r,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{r,j}\},
\]
every query now has specified reference coordinates satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde v_{r,i}:=U^\top v_{r,i}
 \in E+\operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{r,1},\ldots,
       v^{\rm G}_{r,w_{\rm batch}}\}.
 \label{eq:aff:preimage}
\end{equation}
Conditional on all generated variables, including the full Gaussian
draws, leave the unexposed action uniformly distributed subject to the
specified action; generate its values only when needed. Thus unused
Gaussian components impose no further constraint on that action.

To answer the batch, reveal the images under $U$ of
$\Lambda\widetilde v_{r,1},\ldots,\Lambda\widetilde v_{r,w_{\rm batch}}$
according to this conditional law. Since the $u_j$ span the perpendicular
query components,
\[
 E+\operatorname{span}\{\widetilde u_j:1\le j\le k\}
 =E+\operatorname{span}\{\widetilde v_{r,i}:1\le i\le w_{\rm batch}\}.
\]
The specified subspace therefore becomes
\begin{equation}
 E_r=E+\operatorname{span}
       \{\widetilde v_{r,i},\Lambda\widetilde v_{r,i}:1\le i\le w_{\rm batch}\},
 \label{eq:aff:exposed}
\end{equation}
and the returned vectors are exactly
$U\Lambda\widetilde v_{r,i}=Av_{r,i}$.
The remaining action stays conditionally uniform.
Equations~\eqref{eq:aff:preimage}--\eqref{eq:aff:exposed} give
\[
 E_r\subseteq E_{r-1}+\Lambda E_{r-1}
       +\operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{r,i},\Lambda v^{\rm G}_{r,i}:
          1\le i\le w_{\rm batch}\}.
\]
Induction from $E_0=\operatorname{span}\{b_{\rm spec}\}$ yields
\[
 E_r\subseteq
 \operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^j b_{\rm spec}:0\le j\le r\}
 +\sum_{a=1}^r\sum_{i=1}^{w_{\rm batch}}
   \operatorname{span}\{\Lambda^j v^{\rm G}_{a,i}:0\le j\le r-a+1\}.
\]
The degree increases at most once per batch because all its queries
are fixed before any matrix product is returned.

\emph{Outputs and distribution.}
Apply the query construction to the output vectors with independently sampled
$v^{\rm G}_{{\rm out},1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{{\rm out},c_{\rm out}}$,
without applying
$\Lambda$ or returning further answers. Then
\begin{equation*}
 U^\top z_\ell\in E_{T_{\rm depth}}+
   \operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{{\rm out},i}:1\le i\le c_{\rm out}\},
\end{equation*}
which proves~\eqref{eq:aff:krylov}. Complete $U$ uniformly on the
remaining complements. If no unexposed direction remains, or if the
projected queries are linearly dependent, fewer Gaussian directions
are used; all stated Gaussian vectors are still drawn independently.
Bases are chosen by Gram--Schmidt in the displayed order, discarding
zero residuals, so all constructions are measurable.

Each step uses the conditional law of the original Haar rotation.
Consequently, for every fixed realization of the algorithm's internal
randomness, the completed $U$ has Haar law and the instance, queries,
answers, and outputs have their original joint law. The Gaussian draws
have their independent product law. Neither marginal law depends on
the fixed internal random choices; averaging over those choices proves
the independence assertions in the statement. No independence between
$U$ and the Gaussian collection is asserted or needed.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:aff:chebyshev}
Let
\[
 a_j=\ell_j'(0),\qquad
 a_{\rm sum}=\sum_{j=0}^n|a_j|,\qquad
 \omega_j=\frac{|a_j|}{a_{\rm sum}}.
\]
Then $\omega_j>0$, $\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j=1$, and
$a_{\rm sum}=n/L$. Every real polynomial $\psi$ with
$\deg\psi\le n$ and $\psi'(0)=1$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j\psi(\lambda_j)^2\ge\frac{L^2}{n^2}.
 \label{eq:aff:derivative-certificate}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Set $\phi(z)=\prod_{j=0}^n(z-\lambda_j)$. Since the nodes occur in
nonzero pairs $\lambda_{n-j}=-\lambda_j$, this polynomial is even and
$\phi(0)\ne0$, $\phi'(0)=0$. Differentiating
$\ell_j(z)=\phi(z)/[(z-\lambda_j)\phi'(\lambda_j)]$ at zero gives
\begin{equation*}
a_j=\frac{-\lambda_j\phi'(0)-\phi(0)}{\lambda_j^2\phi'(\lambda_j)}
    =-\frac{\phi(0)}{\lambda_j^2\phi'(\lambda_j)}\ne0.
\end{equation*}
The product
$\phi'(\lambda_j)=\prod_{i\ne j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)$ has exactly
$j$ negative factors. Hence
\[
\operatorname{sign}\phi'(\lambda_j)=(-1)^j,
\qquad
\operatorname{sign}\bigl(a_j(-1)^j\bigr)
  =\operatorname{sign}(-\phi(0)),
\]
so all the terms $a_j(-1)^j$ have the same sign.

Define the Chebyshev polynomials by
$T_0(z)=1$, $T_1(z)=z$, and
$T_{k+1}(z)=2zT_k(z)-T_{k-1}(z)$ for $k\ge1$.
The cosine addition formula gives
$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta)$, so
\[
T_n(\lambda_j/L)=(-1)^j,
\qquad T_n'(0)=n\sin(n\pi/2),
\qquad |T_n'(0)|=n.
\]
For every polynomial $\psi$ of degree at most $n$, the interpolation identity
\[
\psi(z)=\sum_{j=0}^n\psi(\lambda_j)\ell_j(z)
\]
holds: the two sides have degree at most $n$ and agree at $n+1$ distinct
points. We can calculate $a_{\text{sum}}$ by applying this identity to $\psi(z)=T_n(z/L)$ and differentiating at zero:
\[
\frac nL
=\left|\frac{T_n'(0)}L\right|
=\left|\sum_{j=0}^na_j(-1)^j\right|
=\sum_{j=0}^n|a_j|=a_{\rm sum}.
\]
It follows that the $\omega_j$ are positive and sum to one. For an
admissible $\psi$, the same interpolation identity and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\begin{align*}
1
&=\psi'(0)^2
  =\left(\sum_{j=0}^na_j\psi(\lambda_j)\right)^2\le\left(\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{a_j^2}{\omega_j}\right)
      \left(\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j\psi(\lambda_j)^2\right)=a_{\rm sum}^2\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j\psi(\lambda_j)^2.
\end{align*}
This proves~\eqref{eq:aff:derivative-certificate}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:dimref:projector}
Let $t,h\ge1$ and $s_{\rm G}\ge0$ be integers. For each
$j=1,\ldots,t$, let
\[
S_j=\operatorname{span}\{v^{\rm G}_{j,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{j,s_{\rm G}}\}
\subseteq\mathbb R^h,
\]
where $v^{\rm G}_{j,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{j,s_{\rm G}}$ are independent
$\mathcal N(0,I_h)$ vectors for each fixed $j$.
The collections corresponding to different indices $j$ may be
dependent. Let $e_1,\ldots,e_t\in\mathbb R^h$ be deterministic unit
vectors, and define
\[
p_j^{\rm proj}=\|\Pi_{S_j}e_j\|^2\in[0,1],
\]
where $\Pi_{S_j}$ denotes the orthogonal projector onto $S_j$.

If $h\ge16s_{\rm G}$, then
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}>\frac12\right\}
\le2te^{-h/32}.
\label{eq:dimref:tail}
\end{equation}
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}
h\ge\max\{16s_{\rm G},32\log(8t)\},
\label{eq:dimref:dimension-condition}
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
\mathbb E\sqrt{1-\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}}
\ge\frac3{4\sqrt2}>\frac12.
\label{eq:dimref:factor}
\end{equation}
For $s_{\rm G}=0$, we use the convention $S_j=\{0\}$.
Then $p_j^{\rm proj}=0$, and the expectation
in~\eqref{eq:dimref:factor} equals one for every $h\ge1$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The case $s_{\rm G}=0$ is immediate. Assume henceforth that
$s_{\rm G}\ge1$ and $h\ge16s_{\rm G}$.

\emph{Step 1: distribution of a single projection.}
Fix $j\in\{1,\ldots,t\}$. Since $s_{\rm G}<h$, the vectors
$v^{\rm G}_{j,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{j,s_{\rm G}}$ are linearly independent
almost surely.
Indeed, conditional on the preceding vectors, each new Gaussian vector
has probability zero of belonging to their proper linear span.
Thus $\dim S_j=s_{\rm G}$ almost surely.

For every deterministic orthogonal matrix $V$, rotational invariance
of the Gaussian distribution gives
\[
(Vv^{\rm G}_{j,1},\ldots,Vv^{\rm G}_{j,s_{\rm G}})
\stackrel{\rm d}=
(v^{\rm G}_{j,1},\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{j,s_{\rm G}}).
\]
Hence $VS_j\stackrel{\rm d}=S_j$, so $S_j$ is uniformly distributed
over the $s_{\rm G}$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb R^h$.
If $U_{\rm Haar}$ is a Haar-distributed orthogonal matrix of order $h$,
then
\[
\Pi_{S_j}\stackrel{\rm d}=
U_{\rm Haar}\begin{pmatrix}
I_{s_{\rm G}}&0\\
0&0
\end{pmatrix}U_{\rm Haar}^\top.
\]
Since an orthogonal projector satisfies
$\Pi_{S_j}^\top\Pi_{S_j}=\Pi_{S_j}$, it follows that
\[
p_j^{\rm proj}
=e_j^\top\Pi_{S_j}e_j
\stackrel{\rm d}=
\sum_{i=1}^{s_{\rm G}}(U_{\rm Haar}^\top e_j)_i^2.
\]

Because $e_j$ is a deterministic unit vector,
$U_{\rm Haar}^\top e_j$ is uniform
on the unit sphere. A standard Gaussian vector normalized by its norm
has the same distribution. Therefore, for independent
$\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_h\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$,
\[
U_{\rm Haar}^\top e_j\stackrel{\rm d}=
\frac{(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_h)^\top}
     {\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^h\zeta_i^2}},
\qquad
p_j^{\rm proj}\stackrel{\rm d}=\frac{S_{\rm num}}{S_{\rm den}},
\]
where
\[
S_{\rm num}:=\sum_{i=1}^{s_{\rm G}}\zeta_i^2,
\qquad
S_{\rm den}:=\sum_{i=1}^h\zeta_i^2>0
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
These identities describe the marginal distribution for the fixed
index $j$; they impose no independence across the different subspaces.

\emph{Step 2: reduction to two scalar tail bounds.}
On the event $\{S_{\rm num}\le h/4\}\cap\{S_{\rm den}\ge h/2\}$, we have
\[
\frac{S_{\rm num}}{S_{\rm den}}\le\frac{h/4}{h/2}=\frac12.
\]
Taking complements gives
\[
\{S_{\rm num}/S_{\rm den}>1/2\}
\subseteq
\{S_{\rm num}>h/4\}\cup\{S_{\rm den}<h/2\}.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb{P}\{p_j^{\rm proj}>1/2\}
\le
\mathbb{P}\{S_{\rm num}>h/4\}
+
\mathbb{P}\{S_{\rm den}<h/2\}.
\]
No independence between $S_{\rm num}$ and $S_{\rm den}$ is needed for this inequality.

\emph{Step 3: exponential bounds for the scalar tails.}
For $S_{\rm chi}=\sum_{i=1}^k\eta_i^2$, where
$\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_k$ are independent $\mathcal N(0,1)$ variables,
independence gives, for every $a<1/2$,
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E e^{aS_{\rm chi}}
&=\prod_{i=1}^k\mathbb E e^{a\eta_i^2}=\left(
  \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}
  \int_{\mathbb R}e^{-(1-2a)x^2/2}\,dx
  \right)^k
=(1-2a)^{-k/2}.
\end{align*}
The last equality follows by substituting
$u=\sqrt{1-2a}\,x$ in the integral.

Applying Markov's inequality to the nonnegative random variable
$e^{S_{\rm num}/4}$ yields
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\{S_{\rm num}>h/4\}
&=\mathbb{P}\{e^{S_{\rm num}/4}>e^{h/16}\}\le e^{-h/16}\mathbb E e^{S_{\rm num}/4}=e^{-h/16}2^{s_{\rm G}/2}\le\exp\!\left(-\frac h{16}+\frac{h\log2}{32}\right)
\le e^{-h/32},
\end{align*}
where the last line uses $s_{\rm G}\le h/16$ and $\log2\le1$.

For the lower tail of $S_{\rm den}$, the map $z\mapsto e^{-z/2}$ is decreasing.
Consequently, Markov's inequality gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\{S_{\rm den}<h/2\}
&=\mathbb{P}\{e^{-S_{\rm den}/2}>e^{-h/4}\}\le e^{h/4}\mathbb E e^{-S_{\rm den}/2}=e^{h/4}2^{-h/2}\\
&=\exp\!\left[-h\left(\frac{\log2}{2}-\frac14\right)\right]
\le e^{-h/12}
\le e^{-h/32}.
\end{align*}

Combining the two tail bounds, we obtain
\[
\mathbb{P}\{p_j^{\rm proj}>1/2\}\le2e^{-h/32}.
\]

\emph{Step 4: simultaneous control and the expectation bound.}
The union bound gives
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}\!\left\{\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}>\frac12\right\}
&=\mathbb{P}\!\left(
  \bigcup_{j=1}^t\{p_j^{\rm proj}>1/2\}
  \right)\\
&\le\sum_{j=1}^t\mathbb{P}\{p_j^{\rm proj}>1/2\}\\
&\le2te^{-h/32}.
\end{align*}
This proves~\eqref{eq:dimref:tail}, regardless of dependence among
the subspaces.

Under~\eqref{eq:dimref:dimension-condition},
\[
2te^{-h/32}
\le2te^{-\log(8t)}
=\frac14.
\]
Therefore the event
\[
\Omega_{\rm good}:=
\left\{\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}\le\frac12\right\}
\]
satisfies $\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{\rm good})\ge3/4$.
Since $0\le p_j^{\rm proj}\le1$ for every $j$, we have the pointwise bound
\[
\sqrt{1-\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}}
\ge\frac1{\sqrt2}\mathbf 1_{\Omega_{\rm good}}.
\]
Taking expectations yields
\[
\mathbb E\sqrt{1-\max_{1\le j\le t}p_j^{\rm proj}}
\ge\frac1{\sqrt2}\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{\rm good})
\ge\frac3{4\sqrt2}
>\frac12,
\]
which proves~\eqref{eq:dimref:factor}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:dimref:residual}
For the preceding construction, let
$v^{\rm G}_1,\ldots,v^{\rm G}_{s_{\rm G}}$ be
independent standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}$,
where $s_{\rm G}\ge0$ is an integer. Let $d_0\ge0$ be an integer with
$d_0+2\le n$. Consider any possibly random vector of the form
\[
 v=p(\Lambda)b_{\rm spec}
   +\sum_{i=1}^{s_{\rm G}}p_i(\Lambda)v_i^{\rm G},
 \qquad\deg p\le d_0.
\]
The degrees of $p_i$ are unrestricted, and all polynomial coefficients
may depend on the Gaussian vectors and additional randomness.
If~\eqref{eq:dimref:dimension-condition} holds, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E\|\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec}\|
 \ge\frac{3LR_0}{4\sqrt2\,n}>\frac{LR_0}{2n}.
 \label{eq:dimref:residual}
\end{equation}
The weaker lower bound $LR_0/(2n)$ also holds under the alternative
condition $h\ge2ts_{\rm G}$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Define
\[
 S_j=\operatorname{span}\{\Pi_{V_j}v_i^{\rm G}:1\le i\le s_{\rm G}\}
 \subseteq V_j,\qquad
 \Pi_j=\Pi_{S_j},\qquad
 p_j^{\rm proj}=\|\Pi_je_j\|^2.
\]
For each fixed $j$, the vectors $\Pi_{V_j}v_i^{\rm G}$ are independent
standard
Gaussians in $V_j$. Because $\Lambda$ acts as $\lambda_jI$ on this
subspace, every real polynomial $q$ satisfies
\[
 \Pi_{V_j}q(\Lambda)y=q(\lambda_j)\Pi_{V_j}y
 \quad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \Pi_{V_j}(\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec})
 &=R_0\sqrt{\omega_j}
        [\lambda_j^2p(\lambda_j)+\lambda_j]e_j
   +\sum_{i=1}^{s_{\rm G}}\lambda_jp_i(\lambda_j)\Pi_{V_j}v_i^{\rm G}.
\end{align*}
The sum belongs to $S_j$, irrespective of its coefficients and degrees.
Applying $I-\Pi_j$ gives
\[
 (I-\Pi_j)\Pi_{V_j}(\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec})
 =R_0\sqrt{\omega_j}\psi(\lambda_j)(I-\Pi_j)e_j,
 \qquad \psi(\lambda)=\lambda+\lambda^2p(\lambda).
\]
For every realization, $\deg\psi\le d_0+2\le n$ and $\psi'(0)=1$.
Since $\|(I-\Pi_j)e_j\|^2=1-p_j^{\rm proj}$, orthogonality of the $V_j$
and~\eqref{eq:dimref:chebyshev} imply
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \|\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec}\|^2
 &=\sum_{j=0}^n\|\Pi_{V_j}(\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec})\|^2\\
 &\ge\sum_{j=0}^n\|(I-\Pi_j)\Pi_{V_j}(\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec})\|^2\\
 &=R_0^2\sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j\psi(\lambda_j)^2(1-p_j^{\rm proj})\\
 &\ge R_0^2(1-\max_j p_j^{\rm proj})
       \sum_{j=0}^n\omega_j\psi(\lambda_j)^2\\
 &\ge\frac{L^2R_0^2}{n^2}(1-\max_j p_j^{\rm proj}).
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:dimref:pointwise}
\end{equation}
This bound is pointwise and hence permits coefficients chosen after
observing all the Gaussian vectors. Taking square roots and then
expectations gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|\Lambda v+b_{\rm spec}\|
 \ge\frac{LR_0}{n}\,\mathbb E\sqrt{1-\max_jp_j^{\rm proj}}.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:dimref:projector}, applied in the $t=n+1$ subspaces $V_j$,
proves~\eqref{eq:dimref:residual}.

Under the alternative condition $h\ge2ts_{\rm G}$ and $s_{\rm G}\ge1$,
each $S_j$ has dimension $s_{\rm G}$ almost surely. Rotational invariance
makes $\mathbb E\Pi_j$ a scalar multiple of $I_{V_j}$; taking its trace gives
\[
 \mathbb E\Pi_j=\frac{s_{\rm G}}hI_{V_j},
 \qquad\mathbb E p_j^{\rm proj}=\frac{s_{\rm G}}h.
\]
Using $\sqrt{1-a}\ge1-a$ for $0\le a\le1$ yields
\[
 \mathbb E\sqrt{1-\max_jp_j^{\rm proj}}
 \ge1-\mathbb E\max_jp_j^{\rm proj}
 \ge1-\sum_{j=0}^n\mathbb E p_j^{\rm proj}
 =1-\frac{ts_{\rm G}}h\ge\frac12.
\]
If $s_{\rm G}=0$, the expectation is one, which proves the same conclusion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:dimref:depth}\label{lem:relmm:depth}
Let $L,R_0>0$ and let $m,T_{\rm depth}$ be positive integers. In dimension
$d_{\rm ref}(m,T_{\rm depth})$, there is a single fixed distribution over noiseless
affine monotone $L$-Lipschitz fields, each with a unique unknown root
$x_\star$ of norm $R_0$. For the root-centered restricted Minty gap
in~\eqref{eq:aff:self-contained-gap},
every randomized algorithm using at most $T_{\rm depth}$ global batches of $m$
simultaneous exact field queries satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)
 \ge\frac{LR_0^2}{2n}\ge\frac{LR_0^2}{6T_{\rm depth}}.
 \label{eq:dimref:depth}
\end{equation}
Queries and outputs are arbitrary finite vectors, and the root is not
given to the algorithm. The instance distribution is independent of the algorithm and its internal randomness; the expectation
is over that distribution and the algorithm's randomness.
In particular, the bound applies to $m$ workers making at most $K$
local queries per worker in each of $N$ communication rounds by taking
$T_{\rm depth}=KN$, where $K,N$ are positive integers. Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
 d_{\rm ref}(m,T_{\rm depth})
 \le\min\{4t^2s_{\rm G},64ts_{\rm G}\}
 \le1024mT_{\rm depth}^2.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Use multiplicity $h=h_{\rm ref}$ in the preceding spectral construction,
so $d_{\rm sym}=th_{\rm ref}$. Draw
\[
 U\sim\operatorname{Haar}(O(d_{\rm sym})),\qquad
 A=U\Lambda U^\top,\qquad b_{\rm rhs}=Ub_{\rm spec},
\]
and, for $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}\times\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sym}}$,
define
\[
 G_A(u,v)=(Av+b_{\rm rhs},-Au),\qquad
 J_A=\begin{pmatrix}0&A\\-A&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The law of $U$, and hence that of $G_A$, is fixed by $L,R_0,m,T_{\rm depth}$.

\emph{Field properties.}
Since $A=A^\top$, the linear part satisfies $J_A^\top=-J_A$. Consequently,
\[
 \langle G_A(x)-G_A(y),x-y\rangle
 =\langle J_A(x-y),x-y\rangle=0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \|J_A(u,v)\|^2=\|Av\|^2+\|Au\|^2,
 \qquad
 \|J_A\|_{\rm op}=\|A\|_{\rm op}=\|\Lambda\|_{\rm op}=L,
\]
so the field is monotone and $L$-Lipschitz.
The nonzero eigenvalues of $\Lambda$ make $A$ invertible. The field $G_A$ therefore has the unique root
\[
 x_\star=(0,-A^{-1}b_{\rm rhs})=(0,-Uz_{\rm spec}),
 \qquad \|x_\star\|=R_0.
\]

\emph{Gap identity.}
For an arbitrary output $x=(u,v)$, write a comparator as
$y=x_\star+h_{\rm cmp}$. Since $G_A(y)=J_Ah_{\rm cmp}$ and
$\langle J_Ah_{\rm cmp},h_{\rm cmp}\rangle=0$,
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(x)
 &=\sup_{\|h_{\rm cmp}\|\le R_0}
       \langle J_Ah_{\rm cmp},x-x_\star-h_{\rm cmp}\rangle\\
 &=\sup_{\|h_{\rm cmp}\|\le R_0}
       \langle h_{\rm cmp},J_A^\top(x-x_\star)\rangle\\
 &=\sup_{\|h_{\rm cmp}\|\le R_0}\langle h_{\rm cmp},-G_A(x)\rangle
   =R_0\|G_A(x)\|\\
 &=R_0\sqrt{\|Av+b_{\rm rhs}\|^2+\|Au\|^2}
   \ge R_0\|Av+b_{\rm rhs}\|.
\end{align*}
The supremum equality uses, for any vector $r_{\rm dir}$ of the same
dimension as $h_{\rm cmp}$,
$\sup_{\|h_{\rm cmp}\|\le R_0}\langle h_{\rm cmp},r_{\rm dir}\rangle
=R_0\|r_{\rm dir}\|$,
which follows from Cauchy--Schwarz and is attained at
$h_{\rm cmp}=R_0r_{\rm dir}/\|r_{\rm dir}\|$ when $r_{\rm dir}\ne0$.

\emph{Information available to the algorithm.}
Give $b_{\rm rhs}$ to the algorithm without charge. An exact field query $(u,v)$
can then be answered by two simultaneous matrix queries:
\[
 (Au,Av)\longmapsto(Av+b_{\rm rhs},-Au)=G_A(u,v).
\]
Thus $T_{\rm depth}$ batches of $m$ field queries can be simulated by
$T_{\rm depth}$ batches of $2m$ matrix queries, followed by two arbitrary output
components $(\widehat u,\widehat v)$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:aff:batched} with width $2m$ and two outputs.
It gives $s_{\rm G}=2mT_{\rm depth}+2$ independent standard Gaussian
vectors $v_1^{\rm G},\ldots,v_{s_{\rm G}}^{\rm G}$ and
\[
 U^\top\widehat v
 =p(\Lambda)b_{\rm spec}
  +\sum_{i=1}^{s_{\rm G}}p_i(\Lambda)v_i^{\rm G},
 \qquad\deg p\le T_{\rm depth}.
\]
Allowing unrestricted degrees for the $p_i$ only enlarges the space
containing the output. Since $n\ge T_{\rm depth}+2$, Proposition~\ref{prop:dimref:residual}
applies with $d_0=T_{\rm depth}$. Either multiplicity in
\eqref{eq:dimref:explicit-dimension} yields
\[
 \mathbb E\|A\widehat v+b_{\rm rhs}\|
 =\mathbb E\|\Lambda U^\top\widehat v+b_{\rm spec}\|
 \ge\frac{LR_0}{2n}.
\]
This use of the proposition is unconditional: the Gaussian vectors have
their independent product law, whereas their dependence on $U$ is
irrelevant to the pointwise inequality~\eqref{eq:dimref:pointwise}.
The joint construction preserves the uniform distribution of $U$, independently of the
algorithm's internal randomness. The gap identity therefore proves the lower bound under
the same fixed instance distribution for every randomized algorithm.
Minimality of $n$ gives $n\le T_{\rm depth}+3$. For $T_{\rm depth}=1$ one has $n=3$;
for $T_{\rm depth}\ge2$ one has $T_{\rm depth}+3\le3T_{\rm depth}$. Hence $n\le3T_{\rm depth}$, proving
\eqref{eq:dimref:depth}.

\emph{Intermittent communication.}
Index the queries of each worker within a round by $k=1,\ldots,K$.
At each global batch the simulator makes the $k$th query of every
worker, padding missing queries by zero. All these queries are determined
by earlier batches. Sharing all responses between batches can only give
more information than the intermittent-communication protocol, which restricts each worker to
its local responses until the end of the round. Thus $N$ rounds are
simulated by $KN$ global batches of width $m$.

\emph{Dimension.}
The definition of $n$ gives
$t=n+1\le2T_{\rm depth}+2\le s_{\rm G}$, and $s_{\rm G}\ge4$.
For $s\ge4$ one has $\log(8s)\le s$: the inequality holds at $s=4$,
and $\frac{d}{ds}[s-\log(8s)]=1-1/s>0$. Therefore
\[
 \log(8t)\le\log(8s_{\rm G})\le s_{\rm G},\qquad
 \left\lceil\max\{16s_{\rm G},32\log(8t)\}\right\rceil
 \le32s_{\rm G}.
\]
It follows that
\[
 d_{\rm ref}=2th_{\rm ref}
 \le2t\min\{2ts_{\rm G},32s_{\rm G}\}
 =\min\{4t^2s_{\rm G},64ts_{\rm G}\}.
\]
Finally, $t\le4T_{\rm depth}$ and
$s_{\rm G}=2mT_{\rm depth}+2\le4mT_{\rm depth}$ imply
$64ts_{\rm G}\le1024mT_{\rm depth}^2$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{nn:trajectory}
Run $T\ge1$ extragradient steps with a constant step size
$0<\gamma\le1/(4L)$ and independently sampled batches of size $b$, starting from $x_0$,
and let $\bar y=\frac1T\sum_{t<T}y_t$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{nn:trajectory-bound}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)
 \le\frac{38}7\cdot\frac{D^2}{\gamma T}
       +\frac{69}{64}\cdot\frac{\gamma\sigma^2}{b}
       +\sqrt{\frac{33}{32}}\cdot\frac{D\sigma}{\sqrt{bT}}.
\end{equation}
For $\gamma=\min\{1/(4L),D\sqrt b/(\sigma\sqrt T)\}$, where the second
entry is $+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{nn:trajectory-optimized}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)
 \le\frac{22LD^2}{T}
     +\frac{8\sigma D}{\sqrt{bT}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
\emph{From the gap to the regret.} For the Minty gap, monotonicity
gives $\langle F(u),y_t-u\rangle\le\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle$, hence
\[
 \operatorname{Gap}^{\rm M}_C(\bar y)
 =\sup_{u\in C}\frac1T\sum_{t<T}\langle F(u),y_t-u\rangle
 \le\sup_{u\in C}\frac1T\sum_{t<T}\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle .
\]
For a saddle operator and $u=(u_x,u_y)\in X\times Y$, convexity of
$\Phi(\cdot,y)$ and concavity of $\Phi(x,\cdot)$ give
$\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle\ge\Phi(y_{t,x},u_y)-\Phi(u_x,y_{t,y})$.
Averaging over $t$ and applying Jensen's inequality to the convex
function $\Phi(\cdot,u_y)$ and the concave function $\Phi(u_x,\cdot)$,
\[
 \Phi(\bar y_x,u_y)-\Phi(u_x,\bar y_y)
 \le\frac1T\sum_{t<T}\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle,
\]
and the supremum over $u$ gives the same bound for
$\operatorname{Gap}^{\rm PD}_{X\times Y}(\bar y)$.

\emph{The regret.} Sum~\eqref{nn:identity} over $t<T$ for a fixed
$u\in C$, drop $-\|x_T-u\|^2$, and write
$x_t-\gamma F(y_t)-u=(x_t-\gamma F(y_t)-x_0)+(x_0-u)$. With
$S_\delta=\sum_{t<T}\delta_t$,
\[
 2\gamma\sum_{t<T}\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle
 \le\|x_0-u\|^2+\gamma^2\sum_{t<T}\mathcal R_{{\rm eg},t}
 -2\gamma\sum_{t<T}\langle\delta_t,x_t-\gamma F(y_t)-x_0\rangle
 +2\gamma\langle S_\delta,u-x_0\rangle .
\]
Since $\|u-x_0\|\le D$, the first and last terms are at most $D^2$ and
$2\gamma D\|S_\delta\|$, and only these depend on $u$. Take the supremum over
$u\in C$ and then the expectation. The third term has zero mean,
because each $\delta_t$ is centered given the vector it multiplies. By
the proof of Lemma~\ref{nn:one-step},
$\mathbb E\mathcal R_{{\rm eg},t}
\le-\frac7{128}\mathbb E\|F(x_t)\|^2+\frac{69}{32}\sigma_b^2$ with
$\sigma_b^2=\sigma^2/b$. Writing
$V_F=\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E\|F(x_t)\|^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{nn:regret-bound}
 2\gamma\,\mathbb E\sup_{u\in C}\sum_{t<T}\langle F(y_t),y_t-u\rangle
 \le D^2-\frac7{128}\gamma^2V_F+\frac{69}{32}\gamma^2T\sigma_b^2
 +2\gamma D\,\mathbb E\|S_\delta\| .
\end{equation}

\emph{The corrector sum.} The errors $\delta_t$ are martingale
differences, so~\eqref{nn:corrector} gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|S_\delta\|^2=\sum_{t<T}\mathbb E\|\delta_t\|^2
 \le\frac{69}{32}\alpha_{\rm rel}V_F+\frac{33}{32}T\sigma_b^2,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\|S_\delta\|\le\sqrt{\frac{69}{32}\alpha_{\rm rel}V_F}
      +\sqrt{\frac{33}{32}T}\,\sigma_b .
\]
For $\alpha,\beta>0$,
$\max_{V_F\ge0}(-\alpha V_F+\beta\sqrt {V_F})=\beta^2/(4\alpha)$.
With $\alpha=\frac7{128}\gamma^2$,
$\beta=2\gamma D\sqrt{69\alpha_{\rm rel}/32}$ and
$\alpha_{\rm rel}\le1/4$,
\[
 -\frac7{128}\gamma^2V_F
 +2\gamma D\sqrt{\frac{69}{32}\alpha_{\rm rel}V_F}
 \le\frac{4\gamma^2D^2\cdot69\alpha_{\rm rel}/32}
          {4\cdot7\gamma^2/128}
 =\frac{276\alpha_{\rm rel}}{7}D^2\le\frac{69}7D^2 .
\]
Substituting into~\eqref{nn:regret-bound} and dividing by $2\gamma T$,
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)
 \le\Bigl(1+\frac{69}7\Bigr)\frac{D^2}{2\gamma T}
 +\frac{69}{64}\gamma\sigma_b^2
 +\sqrt{\frac{33}{32}}\cdot\frac{D\sigma_b}{\sqrt T},
\]
which is~\eqref{nn:trajectory-bound}, since $(1+69/7)/2=38/7$.

\emph{The step size.} For the given $\gamma$,
$1/\gamma\le4L+\sigma\sqrt T/(D\sqrt b)$ and
$\gamma\sigma^2/b\le D\sigma/\sqrt{bT}$. Substituting,
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)
 \le\frac{152}7\cdot\frac{LD^2}T
 +\Bigl(\frac{38}7+\frac{69}{64}+\sqrt{\frac{33}{32}}\Bigr)\frac{D\sigma}{\sqrt{bT}},
\]
and $152/7<22$, $38/7+69/64+\sqrt{33/32}<8$.

\emph{Integrability.} All second moments are finite by induction on
$t$, since $F$ is Lipschitz and the oracle has finite conditional second
moments. The supremum over the compact set $C$ of a continuous function
of $u$ equals the supremum over a countable dense subset, so it is
measurable.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{nn:all-budget}
Set $C_{\rm gap}:=440$. For all $m,K,N\in\mathbb N$, the better of the initial point and the two
schedules~\eqref{vi:all-budget-schedules}, chosen by their bounds, satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{nn:ic-upper}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\widehat z)\le C_{\rm gap}\min\left\{
 LD^2,\quad
 \frac{\rho LD^2}{KN}+\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt{KN}},\quad
 \frac{LD^2}{N\min\{1,mK/\rho\}}
       +\frac{\sigma D}{\sqrt{mKN}}
 \right\}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
\emph{Initial point.} For $u\in C$, $\|u-z_\star\|\le2D$ and
$\|x_0-u\|\le D$, so
$\operatorname{Gap}^{\rm M}_C(x_0)\le\sup_{u\in C}\|F(u)\|\,\|x_0-u\|\le2LD^2$. For a
saddle operator, convexity--concavity gives, for
$u=(u_x,u_y)\in X\times Y$,
\[
 \Phi(x_{0,x},u_y)-\Phi(u_x,x_{0,y})
 \le\langle F(x_0),x_0-u\rangle\le\|F(x_0)\|D\le LD^2,
\]
since $\|F(x_0)\|\le L\|x_0-z_\star\|\le LD$.

\emph{Serial schedule.} If $KN\ge4b$, then $KN/(2b)\ge2$, so
$T_{\rm sd}\ge KN/(4b)$ and $bT_{\rm sd}\ge KN/4$.
By~\eqref{nn:trajectory-optimized} and $b\le4\rho$,
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)
 \le\frac{88bLD^2}{KN}+\frac{16\sigma D}{\sqrt{KN}}
 \le\frac{352\rho LD^2}{KN}+\frac{16\sigma D}{\sqrt{KN}} .
\]
If $KN<4b\le16\rho$, the initial point gives
$2LD^2\le32\rho LD^2/(KN)$.

\emph{Common queries.} If $N\ge4s_{\rm cq}$, then
$T_{\rm cq}\ge N/(4s_{\rm cq})$ and the total batch size satisfies
$mKs_{\rm cq}T_{\rm cq}\ge mKN/4$.
By~\eqref{nn:trajectory-optimized} and~\eqref{nn:schedule-facts},
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)\le\frac{88s_{\rm cq}LD^2}{N}
      +\frac{16\sigma D}{\sqrt{mKN}}
 \le\frac{440LD^2}{Nw_{\rm cq}}+\frac{16\sigma D}{\sqrt{mKN}} .
\]
If $N<4s_{\rm cq}\le20/w_{\rm cq}$, the initial point gives
$2LD^2\le40LD^2/(Nw_{\rm cq})$.

The three bounds depend only on known parameters, which proves the
claim.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:two-phase-recursion}
Let $d_t\ge0$ satisfy
\[
 d_{t+1}\le(1-\alpha\gamma_t)d_t+v_{\rm rec}\gamma_t^2,
 \qquad v_{\rm rec}\ge0,
\]
for step sizes $0<\gamma_t\le\gamma_0$ with $0<\alpha\gamma_0\le1$. Let
$r_{\rm sw}=\lceil2/(\alpha\gamma_0)\rceil$. If $T\le2r_{\rm sw}$,
take $\gamma_t=\gamma_0$.
Otherwise take $\gamma_t=\gamma_0$ for the first
$T_{\rm const}=\lfloor T/2\rfloor$ steps and
$\gamma_{T_{\rm const}+j-1}=2/[\alpha(r_{\rm sw}+j)]$ for the remaining
steps $j=1,\ldots,T_{\rm dec}$, where $T_{\rm dec}=T-T_{\rm const}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-phase-recursion}
 d_T\le d_0e^{-\alpha\gamma_0T/3}+\frac{14v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2T}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The decreasing steps satisfy
$2/[\alpha(r_{\rm sw}+j)]\le2/(\alpha r_{\rm sw})\le\gamma_0$.
Since $\alpha\gamma_0\le1$, we have
$r_{\rm sw}\le2/(\alpha\gamma_0)+1\le3/(\alpha\gamma_0)$.

\emph{Constant steps.} Unrolling the recursion and using
$1-x\le e^{-x}$,
\[
 d_t\le(1-\alpha\gamma_0)^td_0
      +v_{\rm rec}\gamma_0^2\sum_{j<t}(1-\alpha\gamma_0)^j
 \le e^{-\alpha\gamma_0t}d_0+\frac{v_{\rm rec}\gamma_0}\alpha .
\]
If $T\le2r_{\rm sw}$, then $T\le6/(\alpha\gamma_0)$, so
$v_{\rm rec}\gamma_0/\alpha\le6v_{\rm rec}/(\alpha^2T)$, which
proves~\eqref{eq:two-phase-recursion}.

\emph{Decreasing steps.} Let $T>2r_{\rm sw}$, so $T\ge3$,
$T_{\rm const}\ge T/3$ and $T_{\rm dec}\ge T/2>r_{\rm sw}$.
In the second phase the contraction factors are
$1-2/(r_{\rm sw}+j)=(r_{\rm sw}+j-2)/(r_{\rm sw}+j)$, and their products telescope:
\[
 \prod_{i=j+1}^{T_{\rm dec}}\Bigl(1-\frac2{r_{\rm sw}+i}\Bigr)
 =\frac{(r_{\rm sw}+j-1)(r_{\rm sw}+j)}
        {(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec}-1)(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec})} .
\]
The noise added at step $j$ is
$4v_{\rm rec}/[\alpha^2(r_{\rm sw}+j)^2]$, so its
contribution to $d_T$ is
\[
 \frac{(r_{\rm sw}+j-1)(r_{\rm sw}+j)}
      {(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec}-1)(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec})}
 \cdot\frac{4v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2(r_{\rm sw}+j)^2}
 \le\frac{4v_{\rm rec}}
          {\alpha^2(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec}-1)(r_{\rm sw}+T_{\rm dec})}
 \le\frac{4v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2T_{\rm dec}^2}.
\]
Summing over $T_{\rm dec}$ steps and using the product with $j=0$, which
is at most $r_{\rm sw}^2/T_{\rm dec}^2$,
\[
 d_T\le\frac{r_{\rm sw}^2}{T_{\rm dec}^2}d_{T_{\rm const}}
      +\frac{4v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2T_{\rm dec}}
 \le e^{-\alpha\gamma_0T_{\rm const}}d_0
      +\frac{r_{\rm sw}^2}{T_{\rm dec}^2}
       \cdot\frac{v_{\rm rec}\gamma_0}{\alpha}
      +\frac{4v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2T_{\rm dec}},
\]
where we used $r_{\rm sw}^2/T_{\rm dec}^2\le1$ in front of
$e^{-\alpha\gamma_0T_{\rm const}}d_0$. Since
$r_{\rm sw}\gamma_0\le3/\alpha$ and $r_{\rm sw}<T_{\rm dec}$,
\[
 \frac{r_{\rm sw}^2}{T_{\rm dec}^2}
 \cdot\frac{v_{\rm rec}\gamma_0}\alpha
 \le\frac{3v_{\rm rec}r_{\rm sw}}{\alpha^2T_{\rm dec}^2}
 \le\frac{3v_{\rm rec}}{\alpha^2T_{\rm dec}}.
\]
Hence
$d_T\le e^{-\alpha\gamma_0T/3}d_0
      +7v_{\rm rec}/(\alpha^2T_{\rm dec})$, and
$T_{\rm dec}\ge T/2$
gives~\eqref{eq:two-phase-recursion}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{nn:strong-distance}
Let $F$ be in addition $\mu$-strongly monotone with $0<\mu\le L$, and
let $\|x_0-z_\star\|\le R_0$. One trajectory of $T\ge1$ steps with the
step sizes of Lemma~\ref{lem:two-phase-recursion}, where
$\gamma_0=1/(4L)$ and $\alpha=9\mu/8$. Set
$c_{\rm traj}:=3/32$ and $C_{\rm traj}:=1932/81$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{nn:strong-trajectory}
 \mathbb E\|x_T-z_\star\|^2
 \le R_0^2e^{-c_{\rm traj}\mu T/L}
       +\frac{C_{\rm traj}\sigma^2}{\mu^2bT}.
\end{equation}
Set $c_{\rm sched}:=3/640$ and $C_{\rm sched}:=96$. Consequently, the
better of the initial point and the two schedules~\eqref{vi:all-budget-schedules},
run with these step sizes, satisfies
\begin{align}\label{nn:strong-ic}
 \mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2\le C_{\rm sched}\min\bigg\{&R_0^2,\quad
 R_0^2e^{-c_{\rm sched}\mu KN/(\rho L)}
      +\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2KN},\nonumber\\[-2pt]
 &R_0^2e^{-c_{\rm sched}\mu N\min\{1,mK/\rho\}/L}
      +\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2mKN}\bigg\}
\end{align}
with universal constants shown above.
For $\sigma=0$ this is linear convergence.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
\emph{One step.} Let $d_t=\mathbb E\|x_t-z_\star\|^2$. Conditionally on the
history, $\mathbb E y_t=x_t-\gamma_tF(x_t)$, and since
$\|F(x_t)-F(z_\star)\|\le L\|x_t-z_\star\|$ and $\gamma_tL\le1/4$,
Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \mathbb E\|y_t-z_\star\|^2\ge\|x_t-z_\star-\gamma_t(F(x_t)-F(z_\star))\|^2
 \ge(1-\gamma_tL)^2\|x_t-z_\star\|^2\ge\frac9{16}\|x_t-z_\star\|^2 .
\]
Apply~\eqref{nn:energy} with $u=z_\star$, use
$\langle F(y_t),y_t-z_\star\rangle\ge\mu\|y_t-z_\star\|^2$, and drop the
term $-\frac7{128}\gamma_t^2\|F(x_t)\|^2$:
\begin{equation}\label{nn:distance-recursion}
 d_{t+1}\le\Bigl(1-\frac98\mu\gamma_t\Bigr)d_t+\frac{69}{32}\cdot
 \frac{\sigma^2}b\gamma_t^2 .
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:two-phase-recursion} with $\alpha=9\mu/8$,
$\gamma_0=1/(4L)$ (so $\alpha\gamma_0\le9/32$) and
$v_{\rm rec}=\frac{69}{32}\sigma^2/b$ gives
\[
 d_T\le R_0^2e^{-3\mu T/(32L)}
 +\frac{14\cdot69\cdot64}{32\cdot81}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2bT},
\]
which is~\eqref{nn:strong-trajectory}. The step sizes depend only on $T$
and known parameters, so the bound also holds conditionally on a random
starting point.

\emph{Serial schedule.} If $KN\ge4b$, then $T_{\rm sd}\ge KN/(4b)\ge
KN/(16\rho)$ and $bT_{\rm sd}\ge KN/4$, so
\[
 \mathbb E\|x_{T_{\rm sd}}-z_\star\|^2
 \le R_0^2e^{-3\mu KN/(512\rho L)}+\frac{4\cdot1932}{81}\cdot
 \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2KN}.
\]
If $KN<4b\le16\rho$, then $3\mu KN/(512\rho L)<3/32$, and the initial
point gives $R_0^2\le e^{3/32}R_0^2e^{-3\mu KN/(512\rho L)}$.

\emph{Common queries.} If $N\ge4s_{\rm cq}$, then
$T_{\rm cq}\ge N/(4s_{\rm cq})\ge Nw_{\rm cq}/20$ and the batch size
satisfies $mKs_{\rm cq}T_{\rm cq}\ge mKN/4$, so
\[
 \mathbb E\|x_{T_{\rm cq}}-z_\star\|^2
 \le R_0^2e^{-3\mu Nw_{\rm cq}/(640L)}+\frac{4\cdot1932}{81}\cdot
 \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu^2mKN}.
\]
If $N<4s_{\rm cq}\le20/w_{\rm cq}$, then $Nw_{\rm cq}<20$, and the initial point gives
$R_0^2\le e^{3/32}R_0^2e^{-3\mu Nw_{\rm cq}/(640L)}$.

Since $3/640\le3/512$, $e^{3/32}\le96$ and $4\cdot1932/81<96$, the three
bounds prove~\eqref{nn:strong-ic} with the stated constants.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{vi:all-budget}
Under SGC, the better of the initial point and the two
schedules~\eqref{vi:all-budget-schedules} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{vi:all-gap}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\widehat z)\le\frac{500LD^2}{1+ND_{\mathrm{sched}}}.
\end{equation}
Under strong monotonicity, the endpoint of the schedule with more steps
satisfies
\begin{equation*}
 \mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2
 \le D_0^2\min\left\{1,\ 2\exp\left[-\frac{9N}{320\kappa}D_{\mathrm{sched}}\right]\right\}.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let $z_{\rm sd}=KN/\rho$, $z_{\rm cq}=Nw_{\rm cq}$ with $w_{\rm cq}$
from~\eqref{nn:schedule-facts}, so that
$\max\{z_{\rm sd},z_{\rm cq}\}=ND_{\mathrm{sched}}$.

\emph{Gap.} For $\sigma=0$ and $\gamma=1/(4L)$,
\eqref{nn:trajectory-bound} gives
$\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_C^\diamond(\bar y)\le C_0LD^2/T$
with $C_0=152/7$, and the initial point gives $2LD^2$. Since $b\le4\rho$,
$KN/(2b)\ge z_{\rm sd}/8$. If $z_{\rm sd}\ge16$, then
$T_{\rm sd}\ge z_{\rm sd}/16$ and
\[
 \frac{C_0LD^2}{T_{\rm sd}}\le\frac{16C_0LD^2}{z_{\rm sd}}
 \le\frac{17C_0LD^2}{1+z_{\rm sd}}\le\frac{370LD^2}{1+z_{\rm sd}} ;
\]
if $z_{\rm sd}<16$, then $2LD^2\le34LD^2/(1+z_{\rm sd})$. Similarly,
$s_{\rm cq}\le5/w_{\rm cq}$ gives
$N/(2s_{\rm cq})\ge z_{\rm cq}/10$; if $z_{\rm cq}\ge20$, then
$T_{\rm cq}\ge z_{\rm cq}/20$ and
$C_0LD^2/T_{\rm cq}\le21C_0LD^2/(1+z_{\rm cq})=456LD^2/(1+z_{\rm cq})$,
and if $z_{\rm cq}<20$, then $2LD^2\le42LD^2/(1+z_{\rm cq})$. Taking the
schedule with the larger $z$ proves~\eqref{vi:all-gap}.

\emph{Distance.} For $\sigma=0$ and $\gamma_t=1/(4L)$,
\eqref{nn:distance-recursion} gives
$d_{t+1}\le(1-9/(32\kappa))d_t$. Since $\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x-1$,
$T_{\rm sd}\ge z_{\rm sd}/8-1$ and $T_{\rm cq}\ge z_{\rm cq}/10-1$, so the
larger of the two horizons is
$T\ge ND_{\mathrm{sched}}/10-1$. Hence, using $1-x\le e^{-x}$ and
$e^{9/(32\kappa)}\le e^{9/32}\le2$,
\[
 \mathbb E\|\widehat z-z_\star\|^2\le D_0^2e^{-9T/(32\kappa)}
 \le2D_0^2\exp\Bigl[-\frac{9N}{320\kappa}D_{\mathrm{sched}}\Bigr].
\]
The contraction also gives the bound $D_0^2$, including the case
$T=0$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:clock:simulation}
\label{lem:masked:simulation}
Consider an algorithm of Definition~\ref{def:ic-main} with a masked
oracle, and assume without loss of generality that every worker makes
exactly $K$ calls in every round. Let $Z_{i,r}$ be the number of
informative calls of worker $i$ in round $r$, so that
$Z_{i,r}\stackrel{\rm iid}{\sim}\operatorname{Bin}(K,p)$, and set
\[
 S_{\rm info}=\sum_{r=1}^N\max_{1\le i\le m}Z_{i,r},\qquad
 T_{\rm mask}=\min\bigl\{KN,\ \max\{1,\lceil2N\beta_p\rceil\}\bigr\}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item Conditionally on the indicators, the algorithm can be simulated
by an algorithm that queries the exact operator in $S_{\rm info}$ consecutive
batches of at most $m$ simultaneous queries each.
\item $\mathbb P\{S_{\rm info}\le T_{\rm mask}\}\ge1/2$.
\item Suppose that a fixed distribution of instances gives expected loss
at least $\ell_{\rm dep}\ge0$ to every randomized algorithm that uses at most
$T_{\rm mask}$
batches of at most $m$ exact queries, and that the loss is nonnegative.
Then the same distribution, combined with independent indicators, gives
expected loss at least $\ell_{\rm dep}/2$ to every algorithm of
Definition~\ref{def:ic-main}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
\emph{(i)} Reveal all indicators to the algorithm before it starts.
They are independent of the instance, so this can only help the
algorithm, and from now on every non-informative response is known in
advance. Fix the indicators and a round $r$. For $j\ge1$, the query of
the $j$th informative call of worker $i$ is a function of
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item the information shared at the start of round $r$,
\item the algorithm's randomness and the indicators,
\item the first $j-1$ informative responses of worker $i$ in round $r$,
\end{itemize}
because all non-informative responses in between are known constants.
Put the $j$th informative calls of all workers into one batch. All
queries of batch $j$ are then determined before any response of batch
$j$ is revealed, as required. Round $r$ needs
$\max_iZ_{i,r}$ batches, after which the whole transcript of the round
is known and the communication at its end can be reproduced. Over $N$
rounds the simulation uses $S_{\rm info}$ batches.

\emph{(ii)} By definition of $\beta_p$,
$\mathbb E S_{\rm info}=\sum_{r=1}^N\mathbb E\max_iZ_{i,r}=N\beta_p$, and
$S_{\rm info}\le KN$. If $T_{\rm mask}=KN$, then
$\mathbb P\{S_{\rm info}\le T_{\rm mask}\}=1$. Otherwise
$T_{\rm mask}\ge2N\beta_p$, and Markov's
inequality gives
\[
 \mathbb P\{S_{\rm info}>T_{\rm mask}\}
 \le\frac{\mathbb E S_{\rm info}}{T_{\rm mask}}
 \le\frac{N\beta_p}{2N\beta_p}=\frac12.
\]

\emph{(iii)} Fix the indicators. On the event
$\{S_{\rm info}\le T_{\rm mask}\}$, pad the simulator of~(i) with empty
batches to exactly $T_{\rm mask}$ batches; this is a randomized algorithm
with at most $T_{\rm mask}$ batches of at most $m$ exact
queries. The instance distribution does not depend on the indicators,
so the assumption applies to it:
\[
 \mathbb E[\text{loss}\mid\text{indicators}]\ge \ell_{\rm dep}
 \qquad\text{on }\{S_{\rm info}\le T_{\rm mask}\}.
\]
Since the loss is nonnegative, (ii) gives
$\mathbb E[\text{loss}]\ge
\ell_{\rm dep}\mathbb P\{S_{\rm info}\le T_{\rm mask}\}
\ge \ell_{\rm dep}/2$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:relmm:masked}
Let
\begin{equation*}
 T_{\rm mask}=\min\bigl\{KN,\ \max\{1,\lceil2N\beta\rceil\}\bigr\},\qquad
 d_{\rm hard}=d_{\rm ref}(m,T_{\rm mask})\le1024\,m T_{\rm mask}^2,
\end{equation*}
with $d_{\rm ref}$ from Corollary~\ref{cor:dimref:depth}. There is a
fixed distribution of monotone affine $L$-Lipschitz operators on
$\mathbb R^{d_{\rm hard}}$, each with a unique root at distance $R_0$
from the initial point, and an oracle satisfying SGC with constant
$\rho$, such that every algorithm of Definition~\ref{def:ic-main}
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{pv:minimax-comparison}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)
 \ge\frac{LR_0^2}{12T_{\rm mask}}
 \ge\frac{LR_0^2}{96(1+ND_{\mathrm{info}})}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Translate the initial point to $0$ and take the distribution of
Corollary~\ref{cor:dimref:depth} with $T_{\rm depth}=T_{\rm mask}$.
Against every randomized algorithm with at most $T_{\rm mask}$ batches
of $m$ exact queries it gives
$\mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)\ge LR_0^2/(6T_{\rm mask})$. At every call, the oracle
returns
\[
 \widehat G(x)=\rho B_{\rm mask}G(x),\qquad
 B_{\rm mask}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/\rho)
 \text{ independent of everything else}.
\]
It is unbiased and satisfies SGC with equality:
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat G(x)\mid\mathcal F]=\rho\cdot\frac1\rho\,G(x)=G(x),\qquad
 \mathbb E[\|\widehat G(x)\|^2\mid\mathcal F]=\rho^2\cdot\frac1\rho\,\|G(x)\|^2
 =\rho\|G(x)\|^2.
\]
This oracle is masked with probability $p=1/\rho$, with the known
invertible map $v\mapsto\rho v$ and the constant $0$. The gap is
nonnegative, because the root is an admissible comparator and
$G(x_\star)=0$. Lemma~\ref{lem:clock:simulation}(iii) with
$\ell_{\rm dep}=LR_0^2/(6T_{\rm mask})$ and
$\beta_{1/\rho}=\beta$ gives the first inequality
in~\eqref{pv:minimax-comparison}. For the second, $\lceil x\rceil\le x+1$
gives $T_{\rm mask}\le\max\{1,2N\beta+1\}\le2(1+N\beta)$, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:clock:asymptotic} gives $\beta\le4D_{\mathrm{info}}$. Hence
$12T_{\rm mask}\le24(1+N\beta)\le96(1+ND_{\mathrm{info}})$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:relmm:upper}
There is a universal constant $C_0\ge6$ such that, under SGC and in
every dimension, an algorithm of Definition~\ref{def:ic-main} satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relmm:sharp-upper}
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)
 \le LR_0^2\min\left\{1,\
       \frac{C_0\rho}{NK},\
       \frac{C_0}{N}\Bigl(1+\frac{\rho}{mK}\Bigr)\right\}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The test ball satisfies $B(x_\star,R_0)\subseteq B(x_0,2R_0)$,
because $\|x_0-x_\star\|\le R_0$. Theorem~\ref{nn:all-budget} with
$\sigma=0$, $C=B(x_\star,R_0)$ and $D=2R_0$ therefore gives
an algorithm, combining a serial and a common-query schedule, with
\[
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Gap}_\star^{\rm M}(\widehat x)\le4C'LR_0^2\min\left\{1,\
 \frac{\rho}{KN},\ \frac1{N\min\{1,mK/\rho\}}\right\},
\]
where $C'$ is the constant of that theorem. Since
\[
 \frac1{\min\{1,mK/\rho\}}=\max\Bigl\{1,\frac\rho{mK}\Bigr\}
 \le1+\frac\rho{mK},
\]
the last two entries are covered by~\eqref{eq:relmm:sharp-upper} with
$C_0=\max\{6,4C'\}$. The entry $LR_0^2$ is attained by the initial
point: for $\|u-x_\star\|\le R_0$, monotonicity and $G(x_\star)=0$ give
$\langle G(u),x_\star-u\rangle\le0$, hence
\[
 \langle G(u),x_0-u\rangle
 \le\langle G(u),x_0-x_\star\rangle
 \le\|G(u)\|\,\|x_0-x_\star\|
 \le L\|u-x_\star\|R_0\le LR_0^2.
\]
The algorithm outputs the candidate with the smallest bound; all
bounds depend only on known parameters.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{pv:definition}
Set $z_0=x_0$. In round $r=0,\ldots,N-1$, every worker $i$ starts from
$x_{r,0}^i=z_r$ and performs, for $t=0,\ldots,T-1$,
\begin{align}\label{pv:algorithm}
 y_{r,t}^i&=x_{r,t}^i-\gamma\bigl(G(x_{r,t}^i)+e_{r,t}^i\bigr),\nonumber\\
 x_{r,t+1}^i&=x_{r,t}^i-\gamma\bigl(G(y_{r,t}^i)+\delta_{r,t}^i\bigr),
\end{align}
where $G(x_{r,t}^i)+e_{r,t}^i$ and $G(y_{r,t}^i)+\delta_{r,t}^i$ are
averages of $b$ independent responses at $x_{r,t}^i$ and at $y_{r,t}^i$; the
second batch is drawn after $y_{r,t}^i$ is computed. At the end of the
round the workers communicate and set
\begin{equation*}
 z_{r+1}=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m x_{r,T}^i.
\end{equation*}
The output is
$\widehat y=\frac1{mNT}\sum_{r<N}\sum_{i\le m}\sum_{t<T}y_{r,t}^i$;
each worker keeps the running sum of its points $y_{r,t}^i$ and sends it
at the last communication.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{pv:field-lemma}
Assume SGC and $0<\gamma\le1/(4L)$. Fix a round, condition on its
starting point $z$, and drop the round index. For a worker $i$, let
\[
 d_t=\|M_{\rm eg}^tG(z)\|^2,\qquad
 s_t=\mathbb E\bigl[\|G(x_t^i)\|^2\bigm|z\bigr],
\]
and let $\bar x_t=\frac1m\sum_ix_t^i$. Then $s_t$ does not depend on $i$,
\begin{equation}\label{pv:field-energy}
 \sum_{t<T}s_t\le(1+\vartheta_{\rm grow})^{T-1}\sum_{t<T}d_t,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E\bigl[\|G(\bar x_t)\|^2\bigm|z\bigr]\ge d_t,
\end{equation}
and
$\mathbb E[\|\delta_t^i\|^2\mid z]
\le \alpha_{\rm rel}(1+q_{\rm eg}+q_{\rm eg}\alpha_{\rm rel})\,s_t$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
\emph{Two matrix inequalities.} For every $v$, since
$\langle Jv,v\rangle\ge0$ and $\|Jv\|\le L\|v\|$,
\begin{equation}\label{pv:H}
 \|M_{{\rm eg},1}v\|^2
 =\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle Jv,v\rangle+\gamma^2\|Jv\|^2
 \le(1+q_{\rm eg})\|v\|^2.
\end{equation}
Moreover $M_{\rm eg}=I-\gamma JM_{{\rm eg},1}$. Put
$w=M_{{\rm eg},1}v$, so that $v=w+\gamma Jv$ and
$M_{\rm eg}v=v-\gamma Jw$. Then
\[
 \|M_{\rm eg}v\|^2
 =\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle Jw,w\rangle-2\gamma^2\langle Jw,Jv\rangle
  +\gamma^2\|Jw\|^2
 =\|v\|^2-2\gamma\langle Jw,w\rangle-\gamma^2\|Jv\|^2
  +\gamma^2\|Jw-Jv\|^2.
\]
Since $Jw-Jv=-\gamma J(Jv)$, we have $\|Jw-Jv\|\le\gamma L\|Jv\|$, and
$\langle Jw,w\rangle\ge0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{pv:P}
 \|M_{\rm eg}v\|^2
